why: Kids + families: story-driven history adventures. History facts are a top faceless niche; a recurring time-travelling hero turns facts into a story.

series.name: Tiny Time Traveler
series.style: 3D animated adventure film look, rich historical settings, bright sunlight, dust and golden sparkles when time-travelling, exciting and friendly mood, vertical 9:16 frame
series.negative: text, letters, words, watermark, logo, war, weapons, blood, scary, blurry

characters.name: Zoya
characters.look: Zoya, an adventurous 10-year-old girl with a black ponytail, a yellow hoodie, cargo shorts and a glowing blue wristwatch time machine

characters.name: Tock
characters.look: Tock, a talking brass pocket-watch robot with tiny legs, a round glass face and a bouncy spring tail

rules: Each episode Zoya and Tock travel to one place and time and learn two or three true facts about it.
Only real places and well-known facts, using names, dates and numbers exactly as given in the episode idea. Never invent numbers.
No war, violence or weapons. Be respectful to every culture.
Start with the time-jump sparkle as the hook; end with Tock asking 'Where to next?'.

topics: Giza, Egypt, around 2560 BCE: the Great Pyramid was built from over two million stone blocks and was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Mohenjo-daro in today's Pakistan, around 2500 BCE: a planned city of the Indus Valley with straight streets, covered drains and the Great Bath.
Rome, 80 CE: the Colosseum opened and could hold about 50,000 people, with a giant cloth roof (velarium) for shade.
The Great Wall of China was built and rebuilt over many centuries by different dynasties; most of the wall people visit today was built in the Ming period.
Olympia, Greece, 776 BCE: the first recorded Olympic Games, where the main race was a sprint of about 192 metres.
Machu Picchu, Peru, 1400s: the Inca built this mountain city with stones cut so precisely they fit together without mortar.
Mainz, Germany, around 1440: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press with movable metal type made books much faster to produce.
Kitty Hawk, USA, 1903: the Wright brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight, which lasted 12 seconds.
July 1969: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on it.
Petra, Jordan: the Nabataeans carved a whole city, including the famous Treasury building, straight into pink sandstone cliffs.
Mesopotamia (today's Iraq), around 3200 BCE: one of the first writing systems, cuneiform, pressed into wet clay with a reed.
Taxila in today's Pakistan: an ancient centre of learning on trade routes, and home of the beautiful Gandhara art in stone.
The Karakoram Highway, built between Pakistan and China from 1959 to 1979: one of the highest paved roads in the world.
Xi'an, China, around 210 BCE: the Terracotta Army of about 8,000 clay soldiers, each with a different face, discovered by farmers in 1974.
Paris, 1889: the Eiffel Tower was built for a world fair and was the tallest structure in the world for about 40 years.
moreIdeas: The Vikings, around 800 CE: they sailed long, narrow longships that could cross oceans and also travel up rivers.
Samarkand on the Silk Road: caravans of camels carried silk, spices and paper between China and the Mediterranean.
Angkor Wat, Cambodia, built in the early 1100s: the largest religious monument in the world, surrounded by a huge moat.
Florence, Italy, around 1490: Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, written in mirror writing.
Philadelphia, 1752: Benjamin Franklin's famous kite experiment helped show that lightning is electricity.
Stonehenge, England, around 2500 BCE: giant stones arranged in a circle that line up with the sunrise on the longest day of the year.
Boston, 1876: Alexander Graham Bell made the first telephone call, saying 'Mr. Watson, come here'.
Menlo Park, USA, 1879: Thomas Edison's team made a long-lasting, practical electric light bulb.
Himeji Castle, Japan, completed in 1609: called the White Heron Castle for its shining white walls.
The Pacific Ocean: Polynesian navigators sailed thousands of kilometres between islands without maps, reading stars, waves and birds.
Persepolis, Persia (today's Iran), from around 518 BCE: a grand palace city with staircases carved with people bringing gifts from many lands.
Chichen Itza, Mexico: on the spring and autumn equinox, the sunlight makes a shadow that looks like a snake sliding down the El Castillo pyramid.
England, 1829: George Stephenson's locomotive 'Rocket' won a famous speed trial and helped start the age of railways.
Paris, 1898: Marie Curie and Pierre Curie discovered the elements polonium and radium; in 1903 Marie became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
France, around 1826-1827: Nicephore Niepce took the oldest surviving photograph from a window, and it needed hours of exposure.
